newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook-Brazil weather, US data hold key.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook-Brazil weather, US data hold key.

text.p: Weather conditions and trading data will be key factors for London's coffee and cocoa futures markets this week, when sharp price moves could easily be triggered, traders said on Monday.
The forthcoming New York raws expiry would be instrumental in setting London's tone in white sugar.
For robusta coffee, traders said the market appeared to be taking a much-needed breathing space after the frenetic rally that began in early January.
The focus was as usual on the weather in Brazil. June and July are frost danger months, but so far Brazil's coffee regions have escaped damaging frosts.
"The market is just expecting a frost. Without one, the market will drop," said one European trader.
However, no major cold is in sight over the next three to five days in Brazil's coffee regions, independent forecaster Weather Services Corporation (WSC) said on Monday.
Traders said London's key September contract was likely to move sideways and hover in a broad $1,700-$2,000 range until significant fundamental news emerged.
The market was underpinned by a lack of origin offers, particularly from Indonesia, along with good scale-down buying by manufacturers.

Another big talking point was the size of the coming Brazilian crop as recent estimates issued by the U.S. Department of Agriculture's had been largely discounted by Brazilian officials, producers and many traders.

The USDA pegged Brazil's 1996/97 crop at 27.5 million bags and 28 million for 1997/98. But estimates within Brazil and elsewhere had floated a range of between 20 and 25 million bags for the coming crop.
In cocoa, the net long gain shown in the CFTC Commitments of Traders Report was probably less than the market feared and would probably be neutral to supportive to prices, brokers GNI said.
Traders had said last week that prices were vulnerable to a sell-off if the bi-weekly report showed a sharp increase in speculative long positions.
There had been a sharp build in spec long positions following the rally in the past two weeks.
London and New York dipped on Friday on profit-taking as players were reluctant to go long before the report was released.
London's September contract, pushing to extend a week-long rally, hit a new one-year high of 1,141 stg at one stage on Friday -- but the move soon faltered and prices lurched into negative territory.
Since June 11, the contract has risen by 11 percent on what is seen by many as a purely technical move.
Others have linked the rally to bullish prospects for the coming 1997/98 crop and concerns over the impact of the El Nino weather phenomenon on future harvests.
Some experts said recently that warm ocean temperatures off the western coast of South America had triggered an El Nino weather pattern in the Pacific.
This could bring dry, damaging weather to key cocoa-growing areas such as Indonesia.

In white sugar, traders said the upcoming expiry of New York's July contract would occupy most interest, especially with a heavy fund position and a perceived lack of demand to absorb any physical delivery.
"Obviously July is going to be the focus of attention but you've got to find someone who wants to take delivery," said one trader.

But even though London's spot August contract might move lower in the short term, reacting to a sell-off in New York, seasonal tightness and potentially reduced supply to the end of the year would underpin prices.
"People will buy the forward months because next year is looking a lot tighter that this year," he said. "But that's not to say in the meantime the nears will have some sort of washout."
Technical analysts said London remained bullish, adding that the recent consolidation would be followed by a renewed push higher. Resistance was pegged at $325.00 and then $330.80.
Market sources said liquidation from stale longs was keeping August/October at lower levels but the spread could easily widen again if nearby demand picked up.
That was unlikely while July was still on the board in New York, they said.
"It's quite narrow but whether it pops out at the last moment is a different matter," said another trader.
